title: Aster and the Lonely Cloud
markdown:
Deep in Sunny Slope Valley, autumn winds began to whisper through the trees, and the fields should have burst with plump cheerful pumpkins, big and round and orange, ready for pies and smiling faces. This year the plants drooped. Leaves that ought to have been lively green were a pale weary yellow. They seemed to whisper that they were thirsty. The soil under them had gone crackly. Even the bees sounded dusty. They were thirsty indeed.

Not far from the dry patches lived Aster, a splendid alpaca with a neck so long and soft it was like a woolly periscope. He stretched it high, peeking over the tallest oaks, keeping watch.

One bright breezy morning his fluffy white head bobbed above the treetops and he spotted a cloud. Not a fluffy white sheep of the sky. This one was dull sad gray, drifting without a plan, like a lost balloon, not bringing a single drop.

Oh dear, whispered Aster, nose twitching. That cloud looks as if it has lost its smile.

A tiny shimmer, like a captured sunbeam, caught his eye. Rill the raindrop mage, no bigger than Aster’s smallest hoof-tip, sat on a cheerful daisy. Rill’s hat was a dewdrop, sparkling with tiny rainbows. Rill understood the whispers of wind and the soft sighs of sky, friend to all watery things.

The Wise Owl, voice like old leaves, named them as they were: Rill, friend of every droplet, and Aster, whose eyes could see all the way to the sky.

Rill, light as a feather, scurried up Aster’s woolly leg and sat on his ear, the best spot for secrets. Aster, Rill chirped, voice like a summer shower, that cloud is lost. Very young. Wandered from its family. Lonely. A bit scared. Like a seedling without its plant.

Aster’s long neck drooped in sympathy. The poor thing. And the pumpkin fields so dry. Those plants crying out. Can we help it find its way?

Rill’s dewdrop hat bobbed. We must try. The cloud needs to be brave enough to let rain fall, and brave enough to go home.

They walked toward the gray, Aster’s soft footsteps barely sounding on the dry crackly grass. Kindness, they had found, often begins by going nearer. Closer, a tiny almost-quiet whimpering sigh drifted from inside the cloud, like the softest breath of wind.

Hello, little cloud, Aster called, warm as sunshine on a chilly morning. Are you all right? You look a little sad.

The cloud trembled. Mist swirled at its edges. I’m lost, a watery voice mumbled. I don’t know where to go. I miss mama cloud and papa cloud. But what if I try to rain and it’s only a weak sprinkle. Or a big scary splash that frightens everyone away.

You’re not frightening at all, Rill said, floating nearer with a cheerful buzz. We’re Aster and Rill. The pumpkin fields would love a little rain from you. And your family misses you. I’m quite sure.

The cloud puffed with a spark of hope, then sagged. What if I’m not good enough. What if my rain isn’t the right kind.

Every drop has its purpose, said the Wise Owl, a gentle breeze of a voice. Every cloud, no matter how small, has family waiting.

Aster nudged the cloud with a velvety nose. Look up. He pointed that long neck toward the horizon. In the haze, larger brighter clouds gathered like a hug, fluffy sheep with edges tinged warm. That’s your family. They look as if they’re waiting.

Rill flew higher, a tiny loop-the-loop. They are. Come. A deep calming breath. Let a little rain fall. Aster will be right here. I’ll be cheering.

The cloud hesitated. A wisp of doubt clung to its edges. It thought of the dry yellow pumpkin leaves, curling. It thought of mama cloud, who told stories of how gentle rain made the whole world sparkle and sing. Slowly, hesitantly, the sad gray began to shimmer with a soft hopeful light. A tiny soft shower began to fall. The air grew cool and damp, smelling of fresh earth, and a gentle pitter-patter filled the valley. Not a rumbling storm. A kind helping sprinkle, each drop a little kiss for the earth. The dry ground seemed to sigh with relief. Pale yellow leaves, as if waking from a weary nap, perked ever so slightly and turned their faces toward the gift.

Warmth spread through the little cloud. Not scared. Helping. Then a much larger sunnier cloud, edges like spun gold, drifted close. My little rain shower, a warm rumbling voice, full of joy. We’ve been looking everywhere. How we’ve missed you.

The little cloud, brave now, floated to its mama. Aster and Rill watched, hearts quiet and warm. Nestled in family, the cloud rained a happy steady shower over the pumpkin fields. Plants drank. Leaves opened green. Pumpkins swelled from pale yellow to cheerful rosy orange.

The wandering cloud had found its place, and the valley had color again. Aster and Rill smiled at each other. The forest seemed to sigh, a breeze in the trees. They did not need to say that kindness is large. The pumpkins said it, by being orange, and the little cloud said it, by not being lost.
